Pagination in GraphQL addresses the challenge of fetching large datasets incrementally, moving away from rigid offset-limit patterns that break down under high write concurrency or deep pagination overhead. Relay Cursor Connections is an industry-standard specification defined by Facebook that standardizes how APIs handle pagination, slicing, and traversing large collections of nodes. Unlike offset-based pagination which relies on absolute index numbers, Relay connections use opaque cursors—encoded string pointers representing a specific item's position in a dataset—coupled with edges and pageInfo objects to maintain stable pointers even when items are inserted or deleted concurrently.

The Relay cursor connection specification fundamentally alters how clients interact with graph schemas. A connection object exposes edges (which wrap the actual node data along with the cursor) and pageInfo (containing navigational booleans like hasNextPage, hasPreviousPage, startCursor, and endCursor). This design allows clients to perform forward pagination using first and after parameters, or backward pagination using last and before parameters. By abstracting the storage mechanism behind an opaque cursor, backend developers can easily switch from relational database keyset pagination to time-series streams or distributed indices without modifying the client-facing GraphQL contract.

rows: O(1) access via indexed keyset pointers
O(N) performance degradation deep in the dataset
Immune to missing or duplicate items on concurrent writes
Prone to skipping or duplicating rows if data is mutated
Requires handling opaque cursor strings and edge wrappers

items: Opaque Cursors: Cursors are typically base64-encoded strings containing internal identifiers like database IDs or composite keys (e.g., timestamp + ID), preventing clients from relying on or mutating internal structures.
Edge Wrapping: The 'edges' structure wraps each 'node' alongside its 'cursor', enabling metadata attachment per edge such as relevance scores in search or relationship properties.
PageInfo Invariants: The 'pageInfo' object must accurately reflect boundary conditions using hasNextPage and hasPreviousPage to direct client-side infinite scroll mechanisms safely.
Connection Slice Calculation: Resolvers must fetch limit + 1 items internally to reliably evaluate whether a subsequent page exists without performing expensive COUNT queries.

parsed_answer.content: A common production pitfall in Relay cursor implementations is failing to enforce a maximum value on the `first` or `last` arguments. Malicious or poorly written clients can request `first: 1000000`, bypassing database memory limits and causing OutOfMemoryErrors (OOM) on the JVM heap or massive thread blocking at the database connection pool. Always clamp pagination arguments to a safe upper bound (e.g., max 50 or 100 items per page).
